title: Vocabulary IQ Test Validation: Item Response Theory
text:
Vocabulary is the classic marker of crystallised intelligence, the knowledge that builds up through schooling, reading and experience (Horn & Cattell, 1966). The Vocabulary IQ Test (VIQT) is a 45-item online test from the Open-Source Psychometrics Project. Each item lists five words, and the task is to pick the two words with the same meaning: in tiny, faded, new, large, big the answer is large = big. Respondents were told not to guess, that a wrong answer costs 0.35 points, and that they could answer don’t know instead.
The other tutorials on this site validate self-report questionnaires, where there are no right answers. An ability test is the natural place for item response theory (IRT): items differ in how hard they are and in how sharply they separate people who know a word from people who do not, and IRT puts items and people on one scale. This tutorial calibrates the 45 items with the mirt package (Chalmers, 2012) in 11,961 respondents. It compares the Rasch, two- and three-parameter models, shows how precise the test is at each ability level, tests item fit and differential item functioning, checks the scores against education, native language and age, and finally runs the calibrated items as a simulated computerised adaptive test.


The data come from the Open-Source Psychometrics Project (VIQT_data.zip, 12,173 records collected online between July 2017 and March 2018). The file holds only the people who also completed an optional survey after the test (30 personality statements and five demographic questions), so it is a self-selected group of test takers.
Answer key. The codebook (codebook.txt in the zip) gives the correct answer of every item as a number. An answer is stored as a sum over the selected words: 1 for the first word, 2 for the second, 4, 8 and 16 for the fifth, so 3 means words 1 and 2 and 24 means words 4 and 5. Decoded this way, the codebook key gives a synonym pair for every item (see the item list below). Scoring the data with it reproduces the number of right answers that the test site computed (score_right in the data) for all 12,173 records; data/prepare_viqt.R checks this before it saves the data. The key comes from the codebook, not from the data.
Scoring. An item scores 1 when both correct words were chosen and 0 otherwise: a wrong pair, one or three words, don’t know or no answer at all. This is the number-right score the site reported. Don’t know counts as wrong, not as missing, because it is the answer the instructions asked for when a respondent did not know the pair. People answer don’t know to the items they find hard, so ignoring these answers would reward skipping hard items. The 0.35-point penalty of the site’s formula score is not used. In IRT a wrong answer and a don’t know both mean the respondent did not find the pair, and the model, not a fixed penalty, decides how much a lucky guess is worth (the three-parameter model below tests whether guessing needs its own parameter). The section Don’t know: wrong or missing? shows how much this choice matters.


Code
type <- ifelse(resp == 1, "Correct pair",
        ifelse(codes == -1, "Don't know",
        ifelse(codes == 0, "No response",
        ifelse(codes %in% c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 28), "One or three words", "Wrong pair"))))
type <- factor(type, levels = c("Correct pair", "Wrong pair", "Don't know",
                                "One or three words", "No response"))
knitr::kable(data.frame(table(type), 100 * as.vector(prop.table(table(type)))),
             col.names = c("Answer", "Answers", "%"), digits = 1,
             format.args = list(big.mark = ","), row.names = FALSE)

The test has no built-in validity check: there are no bogus items, and the data have no flag for repeat visits from the same network. data/prepare_viqt.R therefore removes protocols that did not follow the response format, were too fast to have read the items, gave an impossible age, or repeat an earlier record exactly. A few respondents chose a single word on almost every item: they misread the task, so their zeros say nothing about their vocabulary.

title: Vocabulary IQ Test Validation: Item Response Theory
text:
Classical Item Analysis

Score distribution


Code
ggplot(data.frame(total), aes(x = total)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#2166ac", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(total), colour = "#d6604d", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Number right (0-45)", y = "Respondents") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of number-right scores",
          subtitle = "Dashed line: mean")









The test is easy for this sample. The mean is 33.2 of 45 (SD 8.2, median 35), the distribution is skewed to the left (skew -0.75), and 193 respondents (1.6%) answered every item correctly. A ceiling like this limits precision for the best respondents, which the IRT information curve shows directly below.


Item statistics
The proportion correct is the classical item difficulty. The point-biserial correlation relates the item to the total score; the corrected correlation relates it to the total of the other 44 items, so the item does not correlate with itself. For 0/1 items, Cronbach’s alpha is the Kuder-Richardson formula 20 (KR-20; Kuder & Richardson, 1937): \(\text{KR-20} = \frac{k}{k-1}\left(1 - \frac{\sum p_j q_j}{\sigma^2_X}\right)\).


Code
p_item <- colMeans(resp)
r_pb   <- sapply(items, function(j) cor(resp[, j], total))
r_drop <- sapply(items, function(j) cor(resp[, j], total - resp[, j]))
k      <- length(items)
kr20   <- k / (k - 1) * (1 - sum(p_item * (1 - p_item)) / mean((total - mean(total))^2))

# The most common wrong pair (or single word) of each item, as % of all respondents
top_wrong <- sapply(seq_along(items), function(j) {
  w   <- codes[codes[, j] > 0 & resp[, j] == 0, j]
  tab <- sort(table(w), decreasing = TRUE)
  sprintf("%s (%.0f%%)", decode(as.integer(names(tab)[1]), key$words[j]), 100 * tab[[1]] / n_resp)
})
names(top_wrong) <- items

item_stats <- data.frame(item = items, answer = key$answer,
                         p = 100 * p_item, dk = 100 * colMeans(codes == -1),
                         wrong = top_wrong, r_pb = r_pb, r_drop = r_drop)
cat(sprintf("KR-20 = %.3f; corrected item-total r from %.2f to %.2f\n",
            kr20, min(r_drop), max(r_drop)))


KR-20 = 0.921; corrected item-total r from 0.08 to 0.66

KR-20 is 0.92. The items cover a wide range of difficulty, from large = big (99.2% correct) to fractious = querulous (26.8%), but 38 of the 45 items are answered correctly by more than half of the sample.
The lowest item-total correlations belong to the easiest items. The 10 items answered correctly by more than 95% of the respondents have corrected correlations of only 0.08 to 0.22. This comes from the statistic rather than the items: a point-biserial correlation cannot be large when almost everyone gives the same answer. Among the items of medium difficulty (20% to 80% correct), the weakest is Q7 (deal = sale, corrected r = 0.10). Only 47% choose the keyed pair, and the most common wrong answer is claim + recoup (18%). Respondents in the top quarter of the other 44 items choose the keyed pair only somewhat more often than those in the bottom quarter (52% against 39%). Deal and sale are loose synonyms (every sale is a deal, but not every deal is a sale), so the item seems to depend more on how a respondent reads the two words than on how many words they know. Another item to watch is Q26 (annoying = obnoxious): its most common wrong answer, clicker + counter (4%), is arguably a defensible pair as well, since a hand tally counter is also called a clicker.

title: Vocabulary IQ Test Validation: Item Response Theory
text:
Dimensionality
IRT models with one latent trait assume that one ability explains the correlations between the items. Pearson correlations between 0/1 items depend on the item difficulties, so dimensionality is checked on tetrachoric correlations, which estimate the correlation between the continuous tendencies assumed to underlie each pair of right/wrong answers.


Code
tet <- psych::tetrachoric(resp)


Code
eig <- eigen(tet$rho, only.values = TRUE)$values

# Parallel analysis reference: shuffle each item independently (keeps the difficulties,
# removes every correlation) and average the eigenvalues of five shuffled data sets
set.seed(42)
eig_rand <- rowMeans(replicate(5, eigen(psych::tetrachoric(apply(resp, 2, sample))$rho,
                                        only.values = TRUE)$values))


Code
n_pa <- which(eig <= eig_rand)[1] - 1
cat(sprintf("First eigenvalue %.2f (%.0f%% of the variance), second %.2f, third %.2f; ratio first/second %.1f\nFactors above the shuffled-data reference: %d\n",
            eig[1], 100 * eig[1] / k, eig[2], eig[3], eig[1] / eig[2], n_pa))


First eigenvalue 19.29 (43% of the variance), second 3.42, third 1.66; ratio first/second 5.6
Factors above the shuffled-data reference: 3


Code
scree <- data.frame(factor = rep(1:10, 2), eigenvalue = c(eig[1:10], eig_rand[1:10]),
                    source = rep(c("Observed (tetrachoric)", "Shuffled data (mean of 5)"), each = 10))
ggplot(scree, aes(factor, eigenvalue, colour = source)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2166ac", "#d6604d"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  labs(x = "Factor", y = "Eigenvalue") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  ggtitle("Scree plot of the tetrachoric correlations")









One factor dominates: the first eigenvalue is 19.3, 5.6 times the second. Parallel analysis still keeps 3 factors, because with 11,961 respondents the eigenvalues of shuffled data are close to 1 and even trivial factors pass. The question is what the second factor is.


Code
efa2 <- fa(tet$rho, nfactors = 2, n.obs = n_resp, fm = "minres", rotate = "oblimin")
L2 <- unclass(efa2$loadings)
easy_f <- which.max(cor(L2, p_item))             # the factor whose loadings rise with p
colnames(L2)[easy_f]  <- "Easy-item factor"
colnames(L2)[-easy_f] <- "Main factor"
phi2 <- efa2$Phi[1, 2]

load2 <- melt(L2, varnames = c("item", "factor"), value.name = "loading")
load2$p <- p_item[as.character(load2$item)]
ggplot(load2, aes(x = 100 * p, y = loading)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(colour = "#2166ac", size = 2) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = sub("Q", "", item)), size = 2.6, seed = 1, max.overlaps = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~ factor) +
  labs(x = "% correct", y = "Loading (oblimin)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  ggtitle("Two-factor solution of the tetrachoric correlations",
          subtitle = "Each point is an item (labelled by number)")









Code
easy_items <- items[L2[, "Easy-item factor"] >= 0.30 & L2[, "Easy-item factor"] > L2[, "Main factor"]]
weak_both  <- items[apply(L2, 1, max) < 0.30]
native <- !is.na(df_viqt$engnat) & df_viqt$engnat == "Yes"
eig_native <- eigen(psych::tetrachoric(resp[native, ])$rho, only.values = TRUE)$values


Code
cat(sprintf("Items loading at least .30 on the easy-item factor, and more than on the main factor: %d (%.0f%% to %.0f%% correct)\nItems loading below .30 on both factors: %s\nFactor correlation: %.2f\nNative speakers only: first eigenvalue %.2f, second %.2f\n",
            length(easy_items), 100 * min(p_item[easy_items]), 100 * max(p_item[easy_items]),
            paste(weak_both, collapse = ", "), phi2, eig_native[1], eig_native[2]))


Items loading at least .30 on the easy-item factor, and more than on the main factor: 13 (88% to 99% correct)
Items loading below .30 on both factors: Q7
Factor correlation: 0.53
Native speakers only: first eigenvalue 17.48, second 4.12


The two factors do not split the items by content: both hold synonym pairs. They split them by difficulty. The 13 items that load at least .30 on the second factor, and more than on the first, are all among the 14 easiest items of the test (88% to 99% correct), and the two factors correlate 0.53. Q7 (deal = sale) loads weakly on both. A tetrachoric correlation between two items that almost everyone gets right rests on the few people who fail them, and slips or lucky guesses move it a lot. Factors that sort binary items by difficulty have been known in item factor analysis for a long time (Carroll, 1945). The second factor is not a native-language effect either: among native English speakers alone the second eigenvalue is still 4.1. Whether the IRT model, which handles difficulty directly, needs a second dimension is tested with its own fit statistics below.

title: Vocabulary IQ Test Validation: Item Response Theory
text:
Item Response Theory

Three models
All three models give the probability that a person with ability \(\theta\) answers item \(j\) correctly as a logistic curve:
\[P_j(\theta) = c_j + (1 - c_j)\,\frac{1}{1 + \exp[-a_j(\theta - b_j)]}\]

Rasch (1PL) (Rasch, 1960): items differ only in difficulty \(b_j\), the ability at which the probability is 50%; all items share one slope and \(c_j = 0\).
2PL (Birnbaum, 1968): each item also has its own discrimination \(a_j\), the steepness of the curve.
3PL: adds a lower asymptote \(c_j\), the chance that someone with very low ability gets the item right. Picking one of the ten possible pairs at random is right 1 time in 10, but the test discouraged guessing. The lower asymptote is notoriously hard to estimate, so it gets a weak prior, a beta(2, 17) distribution with mean 2/19 ≈ .11, close to that chance rate (the expbeta prior in mirt).

Ability follows a normal distribution with mean 0; its SD is fixed to 1 in the 2PL and 3PL, while the Rasch model estimates it in place of the common slope. The models are fitted by marginal maximum likelihood with the EM algorithm (for the 3PL, maximum a posteriori because of the prior).


Code
fit_rasch <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
fit_2pl   <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
fit_3pl   <- mirt(resp, mirt.model("F = 1-45\nPRIOR = (1-45, g, expbeta, 2, 17)"),
                  itemtype = "3PL", accelerate = "squarem", verbose = FALSE)

models <- list(Rasch = fit_rasch, `2PL` = fit_2pl, `3PL (prior on c)` = fit_3pl)
comparison <- data.frame(model     = names(models),
                         converged = sapply(models, extract.mirt, "converged"),
                         npar      = sapply(models, extract.mirt, "nest"),
                         logLik    = sapply(models, extract.mirt, "logLik"),
                         AIC       = sapply(models, extract.mirt, "AIC"),
                         BIC       = sapply(models, extract.mirt, "BIC"))
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Model", "Converged", "Parameters", "Log-likelihood", "AIC", "BIC"))

Code
lr    <- 2 * (comparison$logLik[2] - comparison$logLik[1])
lr_df <- comparison$npar[2] - comparison$npar[1]
lr_p  <- pchisq(lr, lr_df, lower.tail = FALSE)
cat(sprintf("Likelihood ratio, Rasch against 2PL: chi-square = %.0f, df = %d, p %s\n",
            lr, lr_df, if (lr_p < .001) "< .001" else sprintf("= %.3f", lr_p)))


Likelihood ratio, Rasch against 2PL: chi-square = 14044, df = 44, p < .001


The 2PL is far better than the Rasch model (BIC lower by 13,631): the discriminations range from 0.20 to 3.54, so equal slopes cannot hold. The 3PL lowers BIC by a further 45 points, much less, and it changes the scores very little (the correlation between 2PL and 3PL abilities is shown below). Most lower asymptotes are small (median 0.06); the largest are Q33 (house = domicile, c = 0.37) and Q35 (memorandum = note, c = 0.28). These are items that can be solved by elimination: someone who does not know domicile can still see that carnival, yeast and economy have nothing to do with each other or with house, and pair the two words that are left. The 2PL is used from here on: it fits much better than the Rasch model, and the third parameter adds little.


Overall fit
The likelihood-ratio test compares models with each other; whether a model fits the data at all is tested with the limited-information statistic \(M_2\) (Maydeu-Olivares & Joe, 2006), which compares the observed proportions correct of every item and every pair of items with the model’s predictions.


Code
m2_tab <- rbind(Rasch = M2(fit_rasch), `2PL` = M2(fit_2pl))
knitr::kable(data.frame(model = rownames(m2_tab), m2_tab[, c("M2", "df", "RMSEA", "SRMSR", "TLI", "CFI")]),
             digits = c(0, 0, 0, 3, 3, 3, 3), row.names = FALSE, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),

With 11,961 respondents the \(M_2\) test rejects both models, as any exact test of a model would at this sample size, so the approximate indices are the ones to read. The 2PL fits well (RMSEA 0.030, SRMSR 0.030, CFI 0.983); the Rasch model is clearly worse on every index (SRMSR 0.088).


Local independence
If one ability explains the items, the residuals of any two items (observed minus expected score) should be uncorrelated once ability is taken into account. Yen’s (1984) Q3 is that residual correlation. Its average is slightly negative by construction, so Christensen, Makransky and Horton (2017) suggest judging each Q3 against the average and flagging values more than 0.2 above it.


Code

q3_pairs <- q3[lower.tri(q3)]
cat(sprintf("Q3: mean %.3f, min %.2f, max %.2f; pairs more than 0.2 above the mean: %d of %d\n",
            mean(q3_pairs), min(q3_pairs), max(q3_pairs),
            sum(q3_pairs - mean(q3_pairs) > 0.2), length(q3_pairs)))


Q3: mean -0.015, min -0.21, max 0.14; pairs more than 0.2 above the mean: 0 of 990

ggplot(data.frame(q3 = q3_pairs), aes(q3)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.01, fill = "#2166ac", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(q3_pairs) + 0.2, colour = "#d6604d", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Q3 residual correlation", y = "Item pairs") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  ggtitle("Residual correlations of all 990 item pairs (2PL)",
          subtitle = "Dashed line: mean + 0.2")











Is one dimension enough?


Code
fit_hard <- mirt(resp[, setdiff(items, easy_items)], 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
fs <- fscores(fit_2pl, full.scores.SE = TRUE)       # EAP ability and its standard error
theta <- fs[, "F1"]
r_hard <- cor(theta, fscores(fit_hard)[, 1])
cat(sprintf("Correlation of 2PL abilities from all 45 items with abilities from the %d items outside the easy-item factor: %.3f\nCorrelation of 2PL and 3PL abilities: %.3f\n",
            k - length(easy_items), r_hard, cor(theta, theta_3pl)))


Correlation of 2PL abilities from all 45 items with abilities from the 32 items outside the easy-item factor: 0.997
Correlation of 2PL and 3PL abilities: 0.997


With 11,961 respondents, even small departures from one dimension can be detected, as the tetrachoric analysis did; in practice one dimension is enough. The 2PL reproduces the item pairs closely (SRMSR 0.030), no pair of items shares much residual variance (largest Q3 0.14, for Q24 and Q17), and abilities estimated without the 13 easy items correlate 0.997 with abilities from all 45. The easy-item factor of the tetrachoric analysis does not change who scores high or low.

The discrimination \(a\) is the slope of the curve at its steepest point, on the logistic scale (no 1.7 scaling constant). The most discriminating item is Q24 (lackluster = drab, a = 3.54), and the least discriminating is again Q7 (deal = sale, a = 0.20). Items with very low discrimination get extreme difficulty estimates: Q10 (partner = companion) has b = -7.3, far below any respondent, because its curve is so flat that it reaches 50% only there.


Item characteristic curves
Six items with contrasting properties. The curves are the 2PL predictions; the points are the observed proportions correct in 20 equal-sized groups of respondents ordered by their estimated ability, a visual check of fit.


Code
pick <- c("Easiest"                = items[which.max(p_item)],
          "Hardest"                = items[which.min(p_item)],
          "Most discriminating"    = rownames(pars)[which.max(pars[, "a"])],
          "Least discriminating"   = rownames(pars)[which.min(pars[, "a"])],
          "Worst fit (S-X2 RMSEA)" = itf$item[which.max(itf$RMSEA.S_X2)],
          "Largest c in the 3PL"   = names(which.max(c3)))
pick <- pick[!duplicated(pick)]
panel <- setNames(paste0(names(pick), ": ", item_lab[pick]), pick)

grid <- seq(-4, 3, by = 0.05)
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(pick, function(j)
  data.frame(item = j, theta = grid,
             p = probtrace(extract.item(fit_2pl, j), grid)[, 2])))

groups <- cut(theta, unique(quantile(theta, seq(0, 1, 0.05))), include.lowest = TRUE)
points <- do.call(rbind, lapply(pick, function(j)
  data.frame(item = j, theta = tapply(theta, groups, mean), p = tapply(resp[, j], groups, mean))))

curves$panel <- factor(panel[curves$item], levels = panel)
points$panel <- factor(panel[points$item], levels = panel)
ggplot(curves, aes(theta, p)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2166ac", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = points, colour = "#d6604d", size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 3, labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 32)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = expression("Ability " * theta), y = "P(correct)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  ggtitle("Item characteristic curves (2PL) with observed proportions")









The easiest item is right for almost everyone, so its curve only rises at the far left. The hardest item reaches 50% at θ = 0.82, less than one SD above the average respondent: the test has no truly hard items. The most discriminating item separates people within a narrow band of ability, while the least discriminating one is nearly flat. The observed proportions for the worst-fitting item rise at the lowest abilities and then stay near 90% instead of approaching 1, which the item-fit section below explains. For the item with the largest lower asymptote in the 3PL, the lowest group of respondents lies slightly above the 2PL curve and the next groups slightly below it, the S-shape that a lower asymptote describes. The 3PL’s c = 0.37 itself, though, only dominates the curve below about θ = -2, where only 1.8% of the respondents are, which is one reason lower asymptotes are hard to estimate.


Information and precision
Each item contributes information \(I_j(\theta) = a_j^2 P_j(\theta)[1 - P_j(\theta)]\), which peaks at \(\theta = b_j\) with height \(a_j^2/4\). Test information is the sum over items, and the standard error of an ability estimate is \(SE(\theta) = 1/\sqrt{I(\theta)}\). Because ability has variance 1 in this sample, a standard error of 0.30 corresponds to a reliability of about \(1 - 0.30^2 = .91\).


Code
grid_info <- seq(-4, 4, by = 0.01)
item_info <- do.call(rbind, lapply(items, function(j)
  data.frame(item = j, theta = grid_info, info = iteminfo(extract.item(fit_2pl, j), grid_info))))
item_info$highlight <- item_info$item %in% pick
peaks <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(item_info[item_info$highlight, ], item_info$item[item_info$highlight]),
                               function(d) d[which.max(d$info), ]))

ggplot(item_info, aes(theta, info, group = item)) +
  geom_line(data = item_info[!item_info$highlight, ], colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = item_info[item_info$highlight, ], colour = "#2166ac", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_label_repel(data = peaks, aes(label = item_lab[item]), size = 2.7, seed = 3,
                   min.segment.length = 0, box.padding = 0.4) +
  labs(x = expression("Ability " * theta), y = "Item information") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  ggtitle("Item information curves",
          subtitle = "Blue: the six items of the previous figure; grey: the other 39")











Code
test_info <- testinfo(fit_2pl, matrix(grid_info))
se_curve  <- 1 / sqrt(test_info)
precise   <- range(grid_info[se_curve <= 0.30])
peak_info <- grid_info[which.max(test_info)]
rel_emp   <- empirical_rxx(fs)
rel_marg  <- marginal_rxx(fit_2pl)
cat(sprintf("Information peaks at theta = %.2f (I = %.1f, SE = %.2f); SE <= 0.30 from theta = %.2f to %.2f\nRespondents in that range: %.1f%%; above it: %.1f%%\nEmpirical reliability %.3f, marginal reliability %.3f\n",
            peak_info, max(test_info), min(se_curve), precise[1], precise[2],
            100 * mean(theta >= precise[1] & theta <= precise[2]), 100 * mean(theta > precise[2]),
            rel_emp, rel_marg))


Information peaks at theta = -0.87 (I = 25.2, SE = 0.20); SE <= 0.30 from theta = -2.03 to 0.48
Respondents in that range: 65.7%; above it: 32.7%
Empirical reliability 0.914, marginal reliability 0.909

ggplot(data.frame(theta = grid_info, info = test_info, se = se_curve), aes(theta)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = precise[1], xmax = precise[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey90") +
  geom_line(aes(y = info, colour = "Test information"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = se * scale_se, colour = "Standard error"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.30 * scale_se, colour = "#d6604d", linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Test information` = "#2166ac", `Standard error` = "#d6604d"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Test information",
                     sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / scale_se, name = "Standard error")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 30)) +
  labs(x = expression("Ability " * theta)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  ggtitle("Test information and conditional standard error (2PL)",
          subtitle = "Shaded: SE at or below 0.30 (dotted line)")











Code
wright <- rbind(data.frame(panel = "Respondents (EAP ability)", value = theta),
                data.frame(panel = "Items (2PL difficulty b)", value = pars[, "b"]))
wright$panel <- factor(wright$panel, levels = c("Respondents (EAP ability)", "Items (2PL difficulty b)"))
ggplot(wright, aes(value, fill = panel)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2, colour = "white", boundary = 0) +
  facet_grid(panel ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2166ac", "#d6604d"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = expression("Ability " * theta * " / difficulty b"), y = "Count") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  ggtitle("Person-item map: where the respondents and the items are")









The test is most precise below the average respondent: information peaks at θ = -0.87, where the standard error is 0.20, and the standard error stays at or below 0.30 from θ = -2.03 to 0.48. Above that it rises quickly, to 0.53 at θ = 1.5, because only 7 items have a difficulty above 0 and the hardest has b = 0.82. 33% of the respondents are above the precise range. Averaged over the sample, the scores are reliable (empirical reliability 0.91, marginal reliability 0.91, close to KR-20), but the average hides a test that measures roughly the lower two thirds of this sample much better than the top third. A version of the VIQT for able adults would need harder items, not more items.


Item fit
The S-X2 statistic (Orlando & Thissen, 2000) compares, for each number-right score group, the observed proportion correct on an item with the proportion the model predicts.

26 of the 45 items misfit at p < .05. With 11,961 respondents, this test detects deviations far too small to matter, so the size of the misfit is the better guide. The RMSEA of S-X2 is at most 0.023, so every item follows its curve closely. Even for the three worst items, the observed proportion correct in any tenth of the respondents (ordered by ability) is at most 10 percentage points away from the 2PL prediction (second table).
The three worst items misfit for reasons that can be read from their content. On Q26 (annoying = obnoxious) the proportion correct reaches 90% in the second-lowest tenth of ability and stays between 88% and 93% from there on. Meanwhile the alternative pair clicker + counter grows from 3% in the lowest tenth to 7% at its highest: able respondents see a second answer. Q28 and Q36 have, after Q33 and Q35, the largest lower asymptotes in the 3PL (c = 0.16 and 0.18). Low scorers get them right a little more often, and middle scorers a little less often, than the 2PL predicts. The misfit is real but small. For Q26 it points to the wording of the item; for Q28 and Q36 it is the lower asymptote that the 2PL leaves out, which costs little given how close the 2PL and 3PL scores are.

78% of the respondents used don’t know (or left an item blank) at least once, so the choice matters. Abilities from the two scorings correlate 0.90. The more items someone omitted, the more their score would rise if omissions were ignored: by 0.19 SD on average for one or two omitted items, and by 0.85 SD for 11 or more. Omissions are not random. Across items, the share of don’t know answers correlates -0.89 with the proportion correct, so people omit the hard items. Validity

Mean ability rises with every step of education, from -0.67 (less than high school) to 0.42 (graduate degree). Many respondents without a high-school diploma are teenagers who have not finished school yet, so the comparison is repeated for respondents aged 25 or older. The order stays the same, and the gap between the lowest and highest groups shrinks from 1.09 to 0.67 SD.


Native language


Code
has_lang <- !is.na(d_val$engnat)
d_lang <- cohen_d(d_val$theta[has_lang], droplevels(d_val$engnat[has_lang]))
cat(sprintf("Native speakers: %s, mean %.2f; non-native: %s, mean %.2f; d = %.2f\n",

Native English speakers score much higher than non-native speakers (d = 1.17), as expected for an English vocabulary test.


Age


Code
age_breaks <- c(12, 17, 21, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 90)
age_labels <- c("13-17", "18-21", "22-25", "26-30", "31-40", "41-50", "51-60", "61-70", "71-90")
d_val$age_band <- cut(d_val$age, age_breaks, labels = age_labels)
age_tab <- summ(d_val[has_lang, ], c("age_band", "engnat"))

r_age_native <- cor(d_val$age[d_val$engnat %in% "Yes"], theta[d_val$engnat %in% "Yes"])

Code

  geom_line() +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Yes = "#2166ac", No = "#d6604d"),
                      labels = c(Yes = "Native English speaker", No = "Non-native"), name = NULL) +

  ggtitle("Vocabulary ability by age")









Ability rises steadily with age (r = 0.47). Among native speakers it climbs from -0.67 at ages 13-17 to a peak of 0.82 at 61-70 and levels off after that. Non-native speakers rise with age too, and the gap between the two groups is present at every age. This fits the view of vocabulary as crystallised knowledge that grows through most of adult life (Horn & Cattell, 1966). The data are cross-sectional and self-selected, so the curve mixes ageing with differences between generations and between the kinds of people of each age who take an online vocabulary test.


Differential item functioning by native language
An item shows differential item functioning (DIF) when people of equal ability but from different groups have different chances of answering it correctly. The Mantel-Haenszel procedure (Holland & Thayer, 1988) compares native and non-native speakers within each number-right score group and expresses the common odds ratio \(\alpha_{MH}\) on the ETS delta scale, \(D = -2.35 \ln \alpha_{MH}\). Negative values mean the item is harder for non-native speakers than their total score predicts. ETS classifies items as A (negligible: |D| < 1 or not significant), C (large: |D| ≥ 1.5 and significantly above 1) or B (moderate, everything in between) (Dorans & Holland, 1993).


Code
focal <- df_viqt$engnat[has_lang] == "No"
score <- total[has_lang]
mh <- t(sapply(items, function(j) {
  y <- resp[has_lang, j]
  A <- tapply(y == 1 & !focal, score, sum); B <- tapply(y == 0 & !focal, score, sum)
  C <- tapply(y == 1 & focal, score, sum);  D <- tapply(y == 0 & focal, score, sum)
  N <- A + B + C + D
  R <- A * D / N; S <- B * C / N; P <- (A + D) / N; Q <- (B + C) / N
  # Robins-Breslow-Greenland variance of log(alpha_MH)
  v <- sum(P * R) / (2 * sum(R)^2) + sum(P * S + Q * R) / (2 * sum(R) * sum(S)) + sum(Q * S) / (2 * sum(S)^2)
  c(D = -2.35 * log(sum(R) / sum(S)), SE = 2.35 * sqrt(v))
}))
mh <- data.frame(item = items, answer = key$answer, mh)
mh$ets <- ifelse(abs(mh$D) < 1 | abs(mh$D) / mh$SE < 1.96, "A",
          ifelse(abs(mh$D) >= 1.5 & (abs(mh$D) - 1) / mh$SE > 1.645, "C", "B"))
mh$direction <- ifelse(mh$ets == "A", "Negligible (A)",
                ifelse(mh$D < 0, "Easier for native speakers", "Easier for non-native speakers"))
print(table(ETS = mh$ets, direction = mh$direction))


   direction
ETS Easier for native speakers Easier for non-native speakers Negligible (A)
  A                          0                              0             26
  B                          1                              2              0
  C                          8                              8              0


Code
mh$label <- factor(item_lab[mh$item], levels = item_lab[mh$item[order(mh$D)]])
ggplot(mh, aes(x = D, y = label, colour = direction)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -1, xmax = 1, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey93") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1.5, 1.5), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = D - 1.96 * SE, xmax = D + 1.96 * SE)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Easier for native speakers` = "#2166ac",
                                 `Easier for non-native speakers` = "#d6604d",
                                 `Negligible (A)` = "grey55"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "MH D-DIF (95% CI)", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  ggtitle("Mantel-Haenszel DIF, native against non-native English speakers",
          subtitle = "Grey band: |D| < 1 (A); dashed: |D| = 1.5 (C threshold)")









Code
top_lang <- head(sort(table(df_viqt$country[df_viqt$engnat %in% "No"]), decreasing = TRUE), 8)
cat("Most common countries of non-native speakers:",
    paste0(names(top_lang), " (", top_lang, ")", collapse = ", "), "\n")


Most common countries of non-native speakers: US (375), IN (181), PH (171), DE (145), CA (109), GB (96), NL (73), FR (72) 


16 items show large (C) DIF and 3 moderate (B) DIF, in both directions: of the C items, 8 are harder for non-native speakers than their total score predicts and 8 are easier. The non-native group is diverse; the most common countries are the United States, India, the Philippines and Germany. The pattern is still clear. Items that favour native speakers mostly turn on everyday or informal English words (soar, drab, hanker, crimp, spade, hightail): fly = soar, lackluster = drab, yearn = hanker, crimp = pleat, depression = despondency, shovel = spade, rob = steal, hightail = abscond. Items that favour non-native speakers mostly turn on words of Latin origin that learners meet in school and in formal writing, and that have close relatives in many European languages: incipient = nascent, house = domicile, epistle = letter, bifurcate = fork, partner = companion, memorandum = note, solo = alone, noted = illustrious (compare French domicile, épître, naissant or Spanish domicilio, epístola, naciente). Not every item fits the pattern (despondency is Latinate but favours native speakers), but the split between learned and everyday vocabulary is plain.
DIF of this size does not mean these items are faulty. It means a vocabulary score carries a different mix of word knowledge for native and non-native speakers, and comparisons across the two groups should keep that in mind. Because the DIF runs both ways, it largely cancels in the total score. The matching score contains the DIF items themselves, so the classification is approximate.
The same question in IRT terms: a two-group 2PL in mirt in which the 26 A items are anchors (equal parameters in both groups), the B and C items are free in each group, and the non-native group gets its own mean and variance on the native speakers’ scale.


Code
anchors <- mh$item[mh$ets == "A"]
lang <- factor(as.character(df_viqt$engnat[has_lang]), levels = c("Yes", "No"))  # natives = reference
fit_mg <- multipleGroup(resp[has_lang, ], 1, group = lang, itemtype = "2PL",
                        invariance = c(anchors, "free_means", "free_var"), verbose = FALSE)
mg_no <- coef(fit_mg, simplify = TRUE)$No
cat(sprintf("Non-native speakers on the native speakers' scale: mean %.2f, SD %.2f\n",
            mg_no$means[1], sqrt(mg_no$cov[1, 1])))


Non-native speakers on the native speakers' scale: mean -1.17, SD 1.05


Code
show <- c(c_native$item[1], c_nonnative$item[1])
dif_curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("Yes", "No"), function(g) {
  mod <- extract.group(fit_mg, g)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(show, function(j)
    data.frame(group = g, item = item_lab[j], theta = grid,
               p = probtrace(extract.item(mod, j), grid)[, 2])))
}))
dif_curves$item <- factor(dif_curves$item, levels = item_lab[show])
ggplot(dif_curves, aes(theta, p, colour = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ item) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Yes = "#2166ac", No = "#d6604d"), breaks = c("Yes", "No"),
                      labels = c(Yes = "Native English speaker", No = "Non-native"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = expression("Ability " * theta * " (native speakers' scale)"), y = "P(correct)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  ggtitle("The two items with the largest DIF, by group (multiple-group 2PL)")









At the same ability, a non-native speaker is much less likely to know that fly = soar than a native speaker, and much more likely to know that incipient = nascent. Measured on the anchor items, the non-native speakers are 1.17 SD below the native speakers, close to the difference in single-group scores (d = 1.17), so the conclusion of the native-language comparison above does not depend on the DIF items.

title: Vocabulary IQ Test Validation: Item Response Theory
text:
Adaptive Testing: A Simulation
A calibrated item bank can be given adaptively. A computerised adaptive test (CAT) chooses each next item to be as informative as possible at the current ability estimate and stops once the estimate is precise enough. The CAT with IRT and EAP section of this site builds the adaptive-testing functions in base R, adapted from the catR package (Magis & Raîche, 2012). Here the dichotomous versions run on the VIQT bank, with the 2PL parameters as a 4PL bank with \(c = 0\) and \(d = 1\). Each CAT starts at θ = 0, selects items by maximum Fisher information, estimates ability by EAP (normal prior, 33 quadrature points from -4 to 4; Bock & Mislevy, 1982), and stops when the standard error reaches 0.30 or the 45 items run out.
This is a post-hoc (real-data) simulation: the CAT gives each of 300 randomly chosen respondents the items it selects, and uses the answers that person actually gave to those items. The same respondents calibrated the items, which makes the results somewhat optimistic.


Code
source(paste0(directory, "R/cat_eap_common.R"))
source(paste0(directory, "R/cat_eap_dichotomous.R"))
bank <- cbind(a = pars[, "a"], b = pars[, "b"], c = 0, d = 1)

run_cat <- function(x, se_stop = 0.30) {
  given <- integer(0); est <- 0; se <- Inf
  while (se > se_stop && length(given) < nrow(bank)) {
    given <- c(given, compute_next_item_dichotomous(est, bank, out = given)$item)
    est   <- compute_eap_dichotomous(bank[given, , drop = FALSE], x[given])
    se    <- compute_eap_se_dichotomous(est, bank[given, , drop = FALSE], x[given])
  }
  c(theta = est, se = se, items = length(given))
}

set.seed(42)
sim <- sample(n_resp, 300)
cat_res <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(sim, function(i) run_cat(resp[i, ]))))
cat_res$full_mirt <- theta[sim]
cat_res$full_base <- sapply(sim, function(i) compute_eap_dichotomous(bank, resp[i, ]))
cat_res$reached   <- cat_res$se <= 0.30
cat(sprintf("Full-test EAP, base-R functions against mirt: largest difference %.4f\n",
            max(abs(cat_res$full_base - cat_res$full_mirt))))


Full-test EAP, base-R functions against mirt: largest difference 0.0363


Code
cat(sprintf("Reached SE <= 0.30: %.0f%% of simulees; items used: median %.0f, mean %.1f\nCorrelation of CAT and full-test abilities: %.3f\n",
            100 * mean(cat_res$reached), median(cat_res$items), mean(cat_res$items),
            cor(cat_res$theta, cat_res$full_mirt)))


Reached SE <= 0.30: 68% of simulees; items used: median 13, mean 22.7
Correlation of CAT and full-test abilities: 0.985


Code
cat_res$band <- cut(cat_res$full_mirt, c(-Inf, -1, 0, precise[2], Inf),
                    labels = c("below -1", "-1 to 0", sprintf("0 to %.2f", precise[2]),
                               sprintf("above %.2f", precise[2])))
cat_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cat_res, cat_res$band), function(d)
  data.frame(n = nrow(d), reached = 100 * mean(d$reached), median_items = median(d$items),
             mean_abs_diff = mean(abs(d$theta - d$full_mirt)))))
knitr::kable(data.frame(band = rownames(cat_tab), cat_tab), digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 2), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Full-test ability", "Simulees", "% reaching SE 0.30",
                           "Median items", "Mean |CAT - full|"))

ggplot(cat_res, aes(x = full_mirt, y = items, colour = reached)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = precise[2], linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.8, position = position_jitter(height = 0.3, width = 0, seed = 1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#2166ac", `FALSE` = "#d6604d"), breaks = c("TRUE", "FALSE"),
                      labels = c(`TRUE` = "SE 0.30 reached", `FALSE` = "All 45 items used, SE above 0.30"),
                      name = NULL) +
  labs(x = expression("Full-test ability " * theta), y = "Items administered") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +

  ggtitle("Length of the simulated adaptive test",
          subtitle = "Dashed line: upper end of the range where the full test has SE <= 0.30")









The base-R EAP functions agree with mirt’s full-test scores to within 0.04 (the two use different quadrature grids). In the middle of the bank’s range the adaptive test is short: for simulees with full-test ability between -1 and 0 it reaches a standard error of 0.30 after a median of 9 items, 20% of the test. Towards the edges it needs more items. Above θ = 0.48, where even the full test has a standard error above 0.30, only 11% of the 103 simulees reach the target (EAP standard errors include the prior, so a few just above the line make it). The rest take all 45 items and end where the full test would. At the bottom the shortage is milder: 4 of the 7 simulees below θ = -2.03 reach the target. Overall, 68% of the simulees reach the target, those who do need a median of 10 items, and CAT and full-test abilities correlate 0.985. An adaptive version of the VIQT would save most items for average and below-average respondents, but it cannot fix the shortage of hard items; that needs new items.

title: Vocabulary IQ Test Validation: Item Response Theory
text:
Summary









Evidence
Result




Answer key
Codebook key reproduces the site’s number-right score for all 12,173 records


Classical reliability
KR-20 = 0.92; corrected item-total r 0.08-0.66 (lowest for the easiest items; weakest of medium difficulty: Q7 deal = sale)


Dimensionality
First tetrachoric eigenvalue 19.3 vs 3.4; second factor = 13 of the 14 easiest items; abilities without them r = 0.997


Model choice
2PL over Rasch (BIC lower by 13,631); 3PL adds little (abilities r = 0.997 with 2PL)


Overall fit (2PL)
RMSEA 0.030, SRMSR 0.030, CFI 0.983; largest Q3 0.14


Precision
Empirical reliability 0.91; SE <= 0.30 for theta -2.03 to 0.48; 33% of respondents above that range


Item fit
26 of 45 items p < .05 for S-X2, but RMSEA at most 0.023


Education
Mean ability rises from -0.67 (less than high school) to 0.42 (graduate degree); same order at 25+


Native language
Native speakers higher, d = 1.17; 1.17 SD on DIF-free anchor items


Age
r = 0.47; native speakers peak at 61-70


DIF by native language
16 C items (8 easier for native, 8 for non-native speakers): everyday vs Latin-derived words


Adaptive testing (simulation)
SE 0.30 reached by 68% after a median 10 items; r = 0.985 with the full test

title: RIASEC Validation: Recovering Holland’s Hexagon
text:
Holland’s (1997) theory of vocational interests sorts people and work environments into six types: Realistic (doers: tools, machines, outdoor work), Investigative (thinkers: science and research), Artistic (creators: art, music, writing), Social (helpers: teaching, care, counselling), Enterprising (persuaders: selling, managing) and Conventional (organisers: records, data, procedures). The theory’s distinctive claim is structural: the six types sit on a hexagon in the order R-I-A-S-E-C, so neighbouring types (R and I) correlate more than alternate types (R and A), which in turn correlate more than opposite types (R and S).
This tutorial validates a 48-item public-domain RIASEC measure (eight activities per type) in 75,064 respondents. It goes beyond reliability and factor analysis: it tests the hexagon itself, places university majors in the interest space, and checks the results against published meta-analyses of gender differences and personality correlates.
Respondents rated how much they would like to perform each activity on a 1-5 scale (1 = Dislike, 3 = Neutral, 5 = Enjoy). The questionnaire also contained the Ten Item Personality Inventory (TIPI; Gosling et al., 2003) and a demographic survey with a free-text question on the respondent’s university major.


The data come from the Open-Source Psychometrics Project (RIASEC_data12Dec2018.zip, 145,828 records collected online in 2015-2018). data/prepare_riasec.R applies the cleaning rules below and groups the free-text majors into 16 broad fields; the free text itself is not kept. The most useful rule is built into the questionnaire: a vocabulary checklist asked respondents to tick the words they knew, and three of the sixteen words (cuivocal, florted, verdid) do not exist. A respondent who claims to know a word that does not exist is not reading carefully.

title: RIASEC Validation: Recovering Holland’s Hexagon
text:
Reliability
Cronbach’s alpha and McDonald’s omega (total) for each eight-item scale, with the range of corrected item-total correlations. Omega is computed from a one-factor model of each scale: \(\omega = (\sum\lambda)^2 / [(\sum\lambda)^2 + \sum\psi]\).


Code
reliability <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(factors), function(f) {
  x  <- df[, factors[[f]]]
  a  <- psych::alpha(x, warnings = FALSE)
  l  <- as.vector(fa(x, nfactors = 1, fm = "ml")$loadings)
  data.frame(scale     = f,
             mean      = mean(rowMeans(x)),
             sd        = sd(rowMeans(x)),
             alpha     = a$total$raw_alpha,
             omega     = sum(l)^2 / (sum(l)^2 + sum(1 - l^2)),
             r_drop    = sprintf("%.2f-%.2f", min(a$item.stats$r.drop), max(a$item.stats$r.drop)))
}))

text:
Parallel Analysis


Code
eig <- eigen(cor_mat, only.values = TRUE)$values
cat(sprintf("First eigenvalue: %.2f (%.0f%% of the variance); second: %.2f\n",
            eig[1], 100 * eig[1] / length(eig), eig[2]))


First eigenvalue: 9.07 (19% of the variance); second: 5.71


Code
set.seed(42)
pa <- fa.parallel(df, fm = "ml", fa = "fa", n.iter = 5,
                  main = "Parallel analysis scree plot (RIASEC-48)")









Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors =  10  and the number of components =  NA 


The first eigenvalue stands above the rest. It reflects the general interest factor seen above (how much someone likes activities of any kind), which is one reason interest scores are often read within a person (which type is highest) rather than only across people. It is modest here, and the next five eigenvalues are clearly above 1 as well: the six types, not one general factor, carry most of the structure.
With 75,064 respondents, the random eigenvalues of parallel analysis are almost exactly 1 and very small factors pass the test, so parallel analysis suggests 10 factors. In samples this large it over-extracts; the question is whether the six theoretical factors appear, which the next two sections test.

title: RIASEC Validation: Recovering Holland’s Hexagon
text:
Confirmatory Factor Analysis
A six-factor model in which each item loads only on its own type, the factors are allowed to correlate, and the items are treated as continuous (robust maximum likelihood).


Code
cfa_model <- paste(sapply(types, function(t)
  paste0(t, " =~ ", paste(paste0(t, 1:8), collapse = " + "))), collapse = "\n")
cat(cfa_model, "\n\n")


R =~ R1 + R2 + R3 + R4 + R5 + R6 + R7 + R8
I =~ I1 + I2 + I3 + I4 + I5 + I6 + I7 + I8
A =~ A1 + A2 + A3 + A4 + A5 + A6 + A7 + A8
S =~ S1 + S2 + S3 + S4 + S5 + S6 + S7 + S8
E =~ E1 + E2 + E3 + E4 + E5 + E6 + E7 + E8
C =~ C1 + C2 + C3 + C4 + C5 + C6 + C7 + C8 


Code
cfa_fit <- cfa(cfa_model, data = df, estimator = "MLR", std.lv = TRUE)
fit <- fitMeasures(cfa_fit, c("chisq.scaled", "df", "cfi.robust", "tli.robust",
                              "rmsea.robust", "srmr"))
knitr::kable(data.frame(index = c("Chi-square (scaled)", "df", "CFI (robust)", "TLI (robust)",
                                  "RMSEA (robust)", "SRMR"),
                        value = round(unname(fit), 3)),
             col.names = c("Fit index", "Value"), row.names = FALSE)

302987.212


df

Code
std <- standardizedSolution(cfa_fit)
lam <- std[std$op == "=~", c("lhs", "rhs", "est.std")]
lam$lhs <- factor(type_names[lam$lhs], levels = type_names)

ggplot(lam, aes(x = lhs, y = est.std)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey95", width = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = rhs), size = 2.6, position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, seed = 1)) +
  ylim(0, 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Standardised loading") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  ggtitle("CFA standardised loadings by type")









With 48 items and tens of thousands of respondents, the chi-square test rejects any model, so the approximate fit indices are the ones to read. They disagree: RMSEA and SRMR (0.066 and 0.065) are acceptable, but CFI (0.80) is well below the usual .90-.95 benchmarks. This is the normal result for interest inventories. A strict simple-structure model forbids every cross-loading, yet neighbouring types share activities by design (that is the hexagon), and the general factor adds variance that no single type owns. The EFA above shows where: Perform stunts for a movie or television show (A7) loads almost equally on Artistic, Realistic and Enterprising and is the weakest item in the CFA (standardised loading 0.43). For scoring, what matters is that every item loads clearly on its own type (0.43-0.85).

Randomization test of hypothesized order relations
The hexagon makes 72 predictions about the 15 correlations: each of the 6 adjacent correlations should exceed each of the 6 alternate and the 3 opposite correlations (36 + 18), and each alternate correlation should exceed each opposite one (18). Hubert and Arabie’s (1987) randomization test counts how many predictions hold and compares the count with all 720 ways of assigning the six labels to the hexagon. The correspondence index (CI) is (agreements − violations) / 72, from −1 to +1.


Code
pair_idx <- which(lower, arr.ind = TRUE)

order_test <- function(r, d) {
  rv <- r[pair_idx]; dv <- d[pair_idx]
  pred <- outer(dv, dv, "<")                         # pair p should correlate more than pair q
  diff <- outer(rv, rv, "-")
  c(agree = sum(pred & diff > 0), violate = sum(pred & diff < 0), predictions = sum(pred))
}

observed <- order_test(scale_cor, hex_dist)

perms <- as.matrix(expand.grid(rep(list(1:6), 6)))
perms <- perms[apply(perms, 1, function(p) length(unique(p)) == 6), ]   # all 720 orders
perm_agree <- apply(perms, 1, function(p) order_test(scale_cor[p, p], hex_dist)["agree"])

ci <- (observed[["agree"]] - observed[["violate"]]) / observed[["predictions"]]
cat(sprintf("Predictions met: %d of %d, violated: %d\nCorrespondence index: %.2f\nExact p (%d permutations): %.4f\n",
            observed[["agree"]], observed[["predictions"]], observed[["violate"]],
            ci, nrow(perms), mean(perm_agree >= observed[["agree"]])))


Predictions met: 72 of 72, violated: 0
Correspondence index: 1.00
Exact p (720 permutations): 0.0167


Every one of the 72 predictions holds, so the correspondence index is the maximum of 1. The p-value is as small as this test allows: rotating the hexagon (6 ways) or reflecting it (2 ways) keeps every prediction, so 12 of the 720 labelings fit equally well, and the minimum p is 12/720 ≈ .017. Tracey and Rounds (1993) used this test in a structural meta-analysis of RIASEC correlation matrices and found that the circular order holds across many samples and instruments; this sample is a textbook case.


The hexagon recovered from the data
Multidimensional scaling of the six scale correlations, using no information about the theory, places the types in two dimensions. If Holland is right, they should fall around a circle in R-I-A-S-E-C order.


Code
mds <- cmdscale(as.dist(1 - scale_cor), k = 2)

# Rotate (and reflect if needed) so that Realistic is at the top and the order runs clockwise,
# which only changes the orientation of the plot, not distances
rot <- function(m, a) m %*% matrix(c(cos(a), -sin(a), sin(a), cos(a)), 2)   # rows rotated by a
mds <- rot(mds, pi / 2 - atan2(mds["Realistic", 2], mds["Realistic", 1]))
if (mds["Investigative", 1] < 0) mds[, 1] <- -mds[, 1]

mds_df <- data.frame(type = rownames(mds), x = mds[, 1], y = mds[, 2])
mds_df$angle <- round(90 - atan2(mds_df$y, mds_df$x) * 180 / pi, 6) %% 360
mds_df <- mds_df[order(mds_df$angle), ]
cat("Order going clockwise from Realistic:", paste(substr(mds_df$type, 1, 1), collapse = "-"), "\n")


Order going clockwise from Realistic: R-I-A-S-E-C 


Code
ggplot(mds_df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "#d6604d", alpha = 0.08, colour = "#d6604d", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 4, colour = "#d6604d") +
  geom_label(aes(label = type), nudge_y = 0.05, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.15)) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank(), axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  ggtitle("Holland's hexagon recovered by multidimensional scaling",
          subtitle = "Distances = 1 - r between the six scale scores")









The polygon is not a perfect regular hexagon (no empirical one is: Realistic and Investigative usually sit further apart than the theory implies), but the order around the circle is the test, and it is the one the theory predicts.

title: RIASEC Validation: Recovering Holland’s Hexagon
text:
Majors in the Interest Space
Prediger (1982) showed that the hexagon has two underlying bipolar dimensions: People vs. Things (Social against Realistic) and Data vs. Ideas (Enterprising and Conventional against Investigative and Artistic). Each respondent’s position on these dimensions is the sum of their six z-scores weighted by the cosine and sine of each type’s angle on the hexagon.


Code
w_x <- cos(hex_angle * pi / 180)   # horizontal axis: Data (left) vs Ideas (right)
w_y <- sin(hex_angle * pi / 180)   # vertical axis: Things (top) vs People (bottom)
knitr::kable(data.frame(type = type_names, angle = hex_angle,
                        ideas_vs_data = round(w_x, 2), things_vs_people = round(w_y, 2)),
             row.names = FALSE,

df_riasec$ideas_data    <- as.vector(as.matrix(scores_z) %*% w_x)
df_riasec$things_people <- as.vector(as.matrix(scores_z) %*% w_y)


The 16 major groups come from the free-text answers of the respondents who had attended university. If the scales are valid, each group should sit near the type its field calls for: engineering near Realistic, accounting near Conventional, business near Enterprising, art near Artistic, psychology and education near Social.

has_major <- !is.na(df_riasec$major_group)
majors <- aggregate(cbind(ideas_data, things_people) ~ major_group,
                    data = df_riasec[has_major, ], FUN = mean)

radius <- 1.15 * max(sqrt(majors$ideas_data^2 + majors$things_people^2))

                  x = radius * cos(hex_angle * pi / 180),
                  y = radius * sin(hex_angle * pi / 180))

  geom_polygon(data = hex, aes(x, y), fill = NA, colour = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") +

                  size = 3, seed = 42, min.segment.length = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-radius, radius, 0, 0) * 1.08, y = c(0, 0, radius, -radius) * 1.08,
           label = c("DATA", "IDEAS", "THINGS", "PEOPLE"), colour = "grey50", size = 3, fontface = "bold") +

This is evidence that internal statistics cannot give: the scales separate groups of people who chose different fields, mostly in the directions Holland’s theory predicts. Engineering is Realistic, accounting Conventional, business and economics Enterprising, arts and English Artistic, and psychology, social work and education Social.
Medicine, biology and the physical sciences are Investigative, as expected. The exceptions are informative too: nursing comes out Investigative rather than Social (Social is second), and computer science comes out Realistic. Look at the items: seven of the eight Investigative activities are about biology, medicine or marine life (Study the structure of the human body, Develop a new medical treatment), and there is no item about computing or mathematics, while Assemble electronic parts is a Realistic item. So this Investigative scale is really a life-science scale, and a validity study is also a way of finding out what a scale measures in practice. A mathematics or computing item would broaden it.

title: RIASEC Validation: Recovering Holland’s Hexagon
text:
Gender Differences
Su, Rounds and Armstrong (2009) meta-analysed vocational interests in over 500,000 people and found large differences on the People-Things dimension: men score higher on Realistic (d ≈ 0.84) and women higher on Social (d ≈ −0.68), with d ≈ 0.93 on Things vs People. Positive d means higher scores for men.


Code
mf <- df_riasec$gender %in% c("Male", "Female")
cohen_d <- function(x, g) {
  m <- tapply(x, g, mean); s <- tapply(x, g, var); n <- tapply(x, g, length)
  unname((m["Male"] - m["Female"]) / sqrt(((n["Male"] - 1) * s["Male"] + (n["Female"] - 1) * s["Female"]) / (sum(n) - 2)))
}
g <- droplevels(df_riasec$gender[mf])
gender_d <- data.frame(
  scale = c(type_names, "Things vs People"),
  d = c(sapply(scores[mf, ], cohen_d, g = g), cohen_d(df_riasec$things_people[mf], g)))
gender_d$scale <- factor(gender_d$scale, levels = rev(gender_d$scale))
cat(sprintf("Men: %s, women: %s\n", format(sum(g == "Male"), big.mark = ","),
            format(sum(g == "Female"), big.mark = ",")))


Men: 23,958, women: 50,433

ggplot(gender_d, aes(x = d, y = scale, fill = d > 0)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", d), hjust = ifelse(d > 0, -0.15, 1.15)), size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#2166ac", `FALSE` = "#d6604d"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.2)) +
  labs(x = "Cohen's d (positive = higher for men)", y = NULL) +

The pattern is the one in the meta-analysis: the largest differences are on Realistic and Social and on the Things-People dimension that runs between them, and the other four types differ little. The sizes are smaller, especially for Social. This is a self-selected online sample with twice as many women as men, many of them students of psychology and other social fields, so the men and women here are probably more alike in their interests than in the general population.

title: RIASEC Validation: Recovering Holland’s Hexagon
text:
Interests and Personality
Interests and personality are related but distinct. In the meta-analysis by Barrick, Mount and Gupta (2003), the two strongest links were Extraversion with Enterprising (ρ ≈ .41) and Openness with Artistic (ρ ≈ .39). The TIPI measures each Big Five trait with two items (one reverse-keyed, recoded 8 − x), so its correlations are attenuated by low reliability.


Code
tipi <- df_riasec[, paste0("TIPI", 1:10)]
rev7 <- function(x) 8 - x
big5 <- data.frame(
  Extraversion        = (tipi$TIPI1 + rev7(tipi$TIPI6)) / 2,
  Agreeableness       = (rev7(tipi$TIPI2) + tipi$TIPI7) / 2,
  Conscientiousness   = (tipi$TIPI3 + rev7(tipi$TIPI8)) / 2,
  `Emotional stability` = (rev7(tipi$TIPI4) + tipi$TIPI9) / 2,
  Openness            = (tipi$TIPI5 + rev7(tipi$TIPI10)) / 2,
  check.names = FALSE)

rb <- round(cor(scores, big5, use = "pairwise.complete.obs"), 2)
rb_long <- melt(rb, varnames = c("type", "trait"), value.name = "r")
rb_long$type <- factor(rb_long$type, levels = rev(type_names))

ggplot(rb_long, aes(x = trait, y = type, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#d6604d",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-0.6, 0.6), name = "r") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  ggtitle("RIASEC scales and TIPI Big Five traits")









The correlations are small to moderate (interests are not personality), and the largest ones are where the meta-analysis puts them: Openness with Artistic, Agreeableness and Extraversion with Social, Extraversion with Enterprising. They are smaller than the meta-analytic values, which are corrected for unreliability, while the two-item TIPI scales are short and unreliable.

title: IPIP-NEO-120: Measurement Invariance Across Sex, Countries and Age
text:
Comparing the mean scores of two groups assumes that the questionnaire measures the same thing in the same way in both. Measurement invariance tests that assumption, in a sequence of increasingly strict multi-group confirmatory factor models (Vandenberg & Lance, 2000; Putnick & Bornstein, 2016):








Level
Constraint across groups
What it allows




Configural
Same factor structure
The construct has the same form


Metric (weak)
Equal loadings
Comparing correlations and regressions


Scalar (strong)
Equal loadings and intercepts
Comparing means



If scalar invariance fails, a group difference in observed scores mixes a difference in the trait with differences in how particular items or facets work in each group. Partial invariance (Byrne, Shavelson & Muthén, 1989) frees the intercepts that differ and compares latent means through the indicators that remain invariant. A step is accepted here when it lowers CFI by no more than .010 and raises RMSEA by no more than .015 (Chen, 2007); chi-square tests are not used, because with thousands of respondents per group they reject any constraint.
The questionnaire is the IPIP-NEO-120 (Johnson, 2014): 120 public-domain items from the International Personality Item Pool that measure the 30 facets of the NEO PI-R five-factor model, four items per facet and six facets per domain. Respondents rated each item from 1 (very inaccurate) to 5 (very accurate). The tests below ask whether its scores can be compared between men and women, between 12 countries and between age groups, and what the comparisons show where they are allowed.


Johnson made the 619,150 protocols collected online between 2001 and 2011 freely available on the Open Science Framework, with the scoring key. data/prepare_ipipneo120.R applies the rules below. Johnson had already screened the protocols, so the consistency check (the even-odd index of Johnson, 2005, on the 30 pairs of half-facets) removes very few; most exclusions are incomplete protocols.

title: IPIP-NEO-120: Measurement Invariance Across Sex, Countries and Age
text:
The Five-Factor Structure
Before testing whether the structure is the same across groups, check that it is there: an exploratory factor analysis of the 30 facets in the US sample.


Code
efa <- fa(us[, facet_codes], nfactors = 5, rotate = "oblimin", fm = "ml")
L <- unclass(efa$loadings)
colnames(L) <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(L)), function(j)
  names(which.max(tapply(L[, j], substr(facet_codes, 1, 1), mean))))
L <- L[, names(domains)]
found <- colnames(L)[apply(abs(L), 1, which.max)]
cat(sprintf("Facets whose largest loading is on their own domain: %d of %d\n",
            sum(found == substr(facet_codes, 1, 1)), length(facet_codes)))


Facets whose largest loading is on their own domain: 24 of 30

                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), name = "loading") +
  facet_grid(domain ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0), axis.title = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  ggtitle("Five-factor EFA of the 30 facets (US sample, ML, oblimin)\nValues >= |0.30| shown")









The facets that load more on another domain than on their own each make sense from their content: activity level and assertiveness go with the energetic, goal-directed side of Conscientiousness, self-consciousness with low Extraversion, immoderation (giving in to cravings) with low Conscientiousness, emotionality (openness to feelings) with Neuroticism, and dutifulness shares Conscientiousness with Agreeableness. A one-factor model per domain therefore cannot fit perfectly, which the next step deals with.

title: IPIP-NEO-120: Measurement Invariance Across Sex, Countries and Age
section: Step 1: A Baseline Model for Each Domain
text:
Step 1: A Baseline Model for Each Domain
Invariance is tested on a model that fits in each group, so the first step is a model that fits in the whole sample. Each domain is modelled as one factor measured by its six facet scores. A single factor rarely fits a Big Five domain perfectly, because some facets share variance beyond the domain (Depression and Self-Consciousness, for example, are closer to each other than to Anger). Residual covariances are added from the modification indices in the US sample, the largest first and at most three per domain, and kept fixed in form for all the comparisons.


Code
baselines <- lapply(setNames(names(domains), names(domains)), baseline_model, data = us)
pretty_cov <- function(x) {
  p <- strsplit(x, " ~~ ")[[1]]
  paste(facet_names[p[1]], "with", facet_names[p[2]])
}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  domain = unname(domains),
  cfi0   = sapply(baselines, function(b) b$start[["cfi.robust"]]),
  rmsea0 = sapply(baselines, function(b) b$start[["rmsea.robust"]]),
  added  = sapply(baselines, function(b) paste(sapply(b$added, pretty_cov), collapse = "; ")),
  cfi    = sapply(baselines, function(b) b$final[["cfi.robust"]]),
  rmsea  = sapply(baselines, function(b) b$final[["rmsea.robust"]]),
  srmr   = sapply(baselines, function(b) b$final[["srmr"]])),
  digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Domain", "CFI (one factor)", "RMSEA (one factor)", "Residual covariances added",
                "CFI", "RMSEA", "SRMR"))

Code
# Cohen's d of women minus men, used for the domains and facets below
cohen_d <- function(x, g) {
  m <- tapply(x, g, mean); v <- tapply(x, g, var); n <- tapply(x, g, length)
  unname((m["Female"] - m["Male"]) / sqrt(sum((n - 1) * v) / (sum(n) - 2)))
}
facet_d <- data.frame(facet = facet_codes, d = sapply(facet_codes, function(f) cohen_d(us[[f]], us$sex)))


Metric invariance holds in 5 of the 5 domains: the facets measure the domains with the same loadings for men and women. Full scalar invariance fails in every domain; it holds once some facet intercepts are freed. A freed intercept means that men and women with the same level of the domain score differently on that facet. In Agreeableness, for example, women score much higher than men on Sympathy (d = 0.57), Altruism (0.50) and Modesty (0.45), but not on Trust (0.01), so the facets cannot all share one domain-level difference (the facet chart below).

Latent and observed sex differences
The latent mean difference uses only the invariant facets; the observed difference is the plain difference in the 24-item domain score. Positive values mean higher scores for women.

  latent   = sapply(names(domains), function(dom) latent_means(inv_sex[[dom]], dom)$mean[2]),
  observed = apply(domain_score, 2, cohen_d, g = us$sex))

  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 3, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(latent = "#d6604d", observed = "#2166ac"),
                      labels = c(latent = "Latent (invariant facets)", observed = "Observed domain score"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Standardised difference (positive = higher for women)", y = NULL) +

Code
facet_d$domain <- factor(domains[substr(facet_d$facet, 1, 1)], levels = domains)
facet_d$freed  <- facet_d$facet %in% unlist(lapply(inv_sex, `[[`, "freed"))
facet_d$label  <- factor(facet_label[facet_d$facet], levels = rev(facet_label))
ggplot(facet_d, aes(x = d, y = label, fill = freed)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey65", `TRUE` = "#d6604d"),
                    labels = c(`FALSE` = "Intercept invariant", `TRUE` = "Intercept freed"), name = NULL) +
  facet_grid(domain ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Cohen's d (positive = higher for women)", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) + theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0)) +
  ggtitle("Sex differences in the 30 facets (US sample)")









Costa, Terracciano and McCrae (2001), across 26 cultures, found that women score higher than men on Neuroticism and Agreeableness, and that some facets show differences in the opposite direction to their domain: women higher on openness to feelings, men higher on assertiveness and openness to ideas. The same appears here: women score higher on Emotionality (openness to feelings, d = 0.62), men on Assertiveness (-0.13) and Intellect (openness to ideas, -0.20). The comparison of latent and observed differences is where invariance testing changes the conclusion. For Neuroticism the latent difference (0.65) is larger than the observed one (0.43). For Openness the two even differ in sign: in the observed domain score women score higher (+0.20), because they score higher on the facets whose intercepts had to be freed (Emotionality d = 0.62, Artistic Interests d = 0.34, Liberalism d = 0.16); the latent difference, which rests on the invariant facets (Imagination, Adventurousness, Intellect), slightly favours men (-0.24). Which sex is “more open” depends on which facets are treated as measuring Openness in the same way for both, which is exactly the question measurement invariance answers.

Personality across age
Across age groups, metric invariance fails for Openness: its facets do not relate to the domain in the same way at every age, so its latent age trend below should be read with caution. For the other domains, partial scalar invariance allows latent means to be compared across age groups. The first plot shows them relative to the 14-17 group; the second shows the observed domain scores by single year of age for men and women, smoothed.


Code
age_lm <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(domains), function(dom)
  cbind(domain = domains[[dom]], latent_means(inv_age[[dom]], dom))))
age_lm$domain <- factor(age_lm$domain, levels = domains)
age_lm$group  <- factor(age_lm$group, levels = levels(dat$agegroup))
ggplot(age_lm, aes(x = group, y = mean, colour = domain, group = domain)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#d6604d", "#e6ab02", "#1b9e77", "#2166ac", "#7570b3"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Age group", y = "Latent mean (SD units, 14-17 = 0)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  ggtitle("Latent domain means by age group (US sample, partial scalar models)")











Code
age_obs <- data.frame(age = us$age, sex = us$sex, scale(domain_score))
names(age_obs)[-(1:2)] <- unname(domains)
age_long <- melt(age_obs, id.vars = c("age", "sex"), variable.name = "domain", value.name = "z")
age_mean <- aggregate(z ~ age + sex + domain, data = age_long[age_long$age <= 65, ], FUN = mean)
ggplot(age_mean, aes(x = age, y = z, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.6, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ domain, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Male = "#2166ac", Female = "#d6604d"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Domain score (z)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) + theme(legend.position = "top") +
  ggtitle("Observed domain scores by age and sex (US sample, ages 14-65)",
          subtitle = "Points: mean at each year of age; lines: loess")









The age trends agree with the maturity principle (Roberts, Walton & Viechtbauer, 2006) and with Soto, John, Gosling and Potter’s (2011) cross-sectional study of more than a million internet respondents aged 10 to 65: Agreeableness (latent difference between the oldest and youngest groups +1.39 SD) and Conscientiousness (+0.72) are higher at older ages, and Neuroticism is lower (-0.56). Women score higher than men on Neuroticism and Agreeableness at every age. Openness shows why invariance matters: its latent mean rises into the twenties while the observed score stays almost flat, because the latent mean rests only on the facets whose intercepts were kept equal (Emotionality, Adventurousness, Intellect), while the freed facets (Imagination, Liberalism, Artistic Interests) follow different age trends. These are cross-sectional differences between people of different ages, not changes within people.

title: IPIP-NEO-120: Measurement Invariance Across Sex, Countries and Age
text:
Facet-Level Invariance Map
The domain models above use facet scores. The same tests can be run inside each facet, with its four items as indicators, which is a much stricter look at the items themselves.


Code
facet_step <- function(f, data, group) {
  model <- paste0("F =~ ", paste(key$item[key$facet_code == f], collapse = " + "))
  groups <- levels(droplevels(data[[group]]))
  cfi <- sapply(list(character(0), "loadings", c("loadings", "intercepts")), function(eq)
    fitMeasures(cfa(model, data = data, group = group, group.label = groups, group.equal = eq,
                    estimator = "MLR"), "cfi.robust"))
  data.frame(facet = f, configural = cfi[1], metric = cfi[2] - cfi[1], scalar = cfi[3] - cfi[2])
}
facet_map <- rbind(
  cbind(grouping = "Sex (USA)",      do.call(rbind, lapply(facet_codes, facet_step, data = us,  group = "sex"))),
  cbind(grouping = "Country (12)",   do.call(rbind, lapply(facet_codes, facet_step, data = dat, group = "country"))),
  cbind(grouping = "Age group (USA)", do.call(rbind, lapply(facet_codes, facet_step, data = us,  group = "agegroup"))))

knitr::kable(aggregate(cbind(metric_fails = metric < -0.010, scalar_fails = scalar < -0.010,

At the item level, loadings are equal across groups almost everywhere, but intercepts are not, and least of all across countries. The worst case is Liberalism, whose items ask about voting for liberal or conservative candidates, moral relativism and being tough on crime: what these mean depends on each country’s politics, so neither the loadings nor the intercepts are the same across countries. N3 Depression, E5 Excitement-Seeking, N5 Immoderation fit poorly even before any equality constraint (configural CFI below .95 in at least one grouping), so their four items are not a clean single factor in the first place.
The practical lesson: the domain scores of the IPIP-NEO-120 can be compared across sex, age and these countries at the latent level, using the invariant facets; raw facet scores, and especially raw item scores, should not be compared across countries without testing first.

title: BFI-44 Validation
text:
The Big Five Inventory (BFI-44) was developed by John & Srivastava (1999) as a short measure of the five major dimensions of personality. Participants rated how much each statement applied to them on a scale from 1 (Disagree strongly) to 6 (Agree strongly). The dataset contains 433 respondents.
Items are prefixed by their dimension (Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Neuroticism, Openness) followed by the item number. Items marked R are reverse-scored before analysis.
John, O. P., & Srivastava, S. (1999). The Big Five trait taxonomy: History, measurement, and theoretical perspectives. In L. A. Pervin & O. P. John (Eds.), Handbook of personality: Theory and research (2nd ed., pp. 102–138). Guilford Press.
